blockMcqs.question: What does encapsulation bundle together?
options: A class and its unit tests
Data and the methods that operate on it
Two unrelated classes into one file
A method and its return type
blockMcqs.explanation: Encapsulation bundles an object's fields with the methods that use them, then hides the fields.

blockMcqs.question: Which access modifier allows only the same class to access a member?
options: Public
Protected
Private
Package/default
blockMcqs.explanation: Private restricts access to code inside the same class only.

blockMcqs.question: Who can access a protected member?
options: Only the exact same class
The class and its subclasses
Any code in the program
Only code in a different package
blockMcqs.explanation: Protected widens private to also include subclasses, but not unrelated code.

blockMcqs.question: What can a setter do that a public field cannot?
options: Store more data types
Validate a value before storing it
Make the field faster to read
Remove the need for a constructor
blockMcqs.explanation: A setter is a checkpoint that can reject invalid values; a raw public field has no such check.

blockMcqs.question: In the BankAccount pseudocode, why does the constructor call setBalance?
options: To skip validation on creation
To reuse the same validation rule for the opening value
Because constructors cannot set fields directly
To make balance public
blockMcqs.explanation: Routing the opening balance through setBalance ensures the same negative-balance check applies everywhere, including construction.

blockMcqs.question: Which benefit does encapsulation give when internals change?
options: Callers must update to match new fields
Public methods stay the same, so callers are unaffected
The class must be renamed
Invariants no longer need to be enforced
blockMcqs.explanation: Because callers depend on methods, not internal storage, the class can change its implementation safely.

blockMcqs.question: How do encapsulation and information hiding differ?
options: They are unrelated concepts
Encapsulation is the mechanism; information hiding is the goal
Information hiding only applies to private fields
Encapsulation only works in functional languages
blockMcqs.explanation: Encapsulation is bundling data with methods; information hiding is the goal of keeping details invisible, which encapsulation can fail to achieve if done poorly.

blockMcqs.question: Why is immutability called strong encapsulation?
options: It adds more getters and setters
State can never change after creation, so invariants can't break later
It makes objects visible to all classes
It removes the need for a constructor
blockMcqs.explanation: With no mutation possible after construction, any invariant checked at creation holds forever.

blockMcqs.question: Which is a common encapsulation leak?
options: Making a field private
A getter returning the live internal list directly
Validating input in a setter
Using a constructor to set initial state
blockMcqs.explanation: Returning the actual internal object lets callers mutate it directly, bypassing all of the class's checks.
